title: Tall tented T waves in a missed dialysis session
presentingComplaint: Generalised weakness and nausea after missing two haemodialysis sessions.
history: End-stage kidney disease on haemodialysis three times a week for four years
Missed the last two sessions because of transport problems
Progressive weakness and muscle heaviness over 48 hours
On an ACE inhibitor and spironolactone, both of which raise potassium
symptoms: Generalised muscle weakness, worst in the legs
examinationFindings: Regular slow pulse of normal volume
Reduced power in the proximal muscles with depressed reflexes
Arteriovenous fistula in the left forearm with a good thrill

vitals.bedside: Weak and lethargic with a slow pulse. The tracing here is not a diagnosis of a rhythm — it is a warning about a serum potassium.

ecg.rhythm: Regular, with atrial activity that is present but of very low amplitude
ecg.pWaves: Small and flattened, becoming hard to identify — an early sign of atrial paralysis
ecg.qrs: 0.15 s, broad, with slurring that does not fit any classic bundle branch pattern
ecg.stSegment: Slightly upsloping, merging into the T wave
ecg.tWaves: Tall, narrow-based and symmetrically peaked — 'tented' — most obvious in the precordial leads
keyFindings: Tall, narrow-based, peaked T waves — the earliest and most characteristic change
Flattening of the P waves with PR prolongation as conduction is impaired
Progressive broadening of the QRS without a recognisable bundle branch morphology
The sequence matters: peaked T waves, then P wave loss, then QRS widening, then a sine wave pattern and arrest

interpretation: ECG changes consistent with significant hyperkalaemia: tall peaked T waves, reduced P wave amplitude, PR prolongation and QRS widening. The ECG cannot give a potassium value, and normal-looking tracings occur at dangerous concentrations — treatment decisions rest on the serum result and the clinical picture together.

auscultation.note: Normal heart sounds at a slow rate. Auscultation is unremarkable here — the danger in this case is electrical, not valvular.
No added sounds. Fluid overload from missed dialysis would be sought at the lung bases and in the jugular venous pressure rather than here.

questions.prompt: How would you describe the rhythm?

options.text: A regular bradycardia with low-amplitude atrial activity
options.feedback: Correct. As potassium rises, atrial myocardium becomes inexcitable and P waves flatten before disappearing entirely.

options.text: Atrial fibrillation
options.feedback: The rhythm is regular. Small P waves are still identifiable rather than absent with a chaotic baseline.

options.text: Complete heart block
options.feedback: The P waves that are visible bear a constant relationship to the QRS complexes.

options.text: Ventricular tachycardia
options.feedback: The rate is 58 bpm. The QRS is broad, but this is a bradycardia.

questions.explanation: Hyperkalaemia does not produce one rhythm — it produces a progression of changes. Recognise the pattern, not a single appearance.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes a hyperkalaemic T wave from a normal tall T wave?

options.text: It is narrow-based, symmetrical and sharply pointed
options.feedback: Correct. The shape matters more than the height: a hyperacute ischaemic T wave is broad-based, whereas a hyperkalaemic one is narrow and tented.

options.text: It is simply taller than usual
options.feedback: Height alone is unreliable — tall T waves occur in early repolarisation and in normal young people.

options.text: It is inverted
options.feedback: T wave inversion is not a feature of hyperkalaemia.

options.text: It is always confined to the limb leads
options.feedback: Peaked T waves are usually most obvious in the precordial leads.

questions.explanation: Describe the base as well as the height. Narrow-based and symmetrical suggests potassium; broad-based and asymmetrical suggests ischaemia.

questions.prompt: The QRS is 0.15 s but does not look like either bundle branch pattern. Why?

options.text: Because conduction is slowed diffusely throughout the myocardium, not blocked in one branch
options.feedback: Correct. A raised extracellular potassium concentration depolarises the resting membrane and inactivates sodium channels everywhere, slowing conduction globally.

options.text: Because there is a left bundle branch block
options.feedback: Left bundle branch block gives a broad monophasic R wave laterally with a deep QS in V1 — a recognisable, specific pattern.

options.text: Because the paper speed is wrong
options.feedback: The grid and calibration mark confirm a standard 25 mm/s, 10 mm/mV recording.

options.text: Because of an accessory pathway
options.feedback: Pre-excitation shortens the PR interval and produces a delta wave. The PR interval here is prolonged.

questions.explanation: A broad QRS that fits no bundle branch pattern, especially with peaked T waves, should prompt an urgent potassium measurement.

questions.prompt: Given the missed dialysis, the weakness and this tracing, what is the most likely interpretation?

options.text: Severe hyperkalaemia with cardiac conduction effects
options.feedback: Correct. Missed dialysis, potassium-retaining medication, muscle weakness and this ECG sequence together make hyperkalaemia overwhelmingly likely.

options.text: Acute myocardial infarction
options.feedback: The T waves are narrow-based and tented rather than broad and hyperacute, there is no ST elevation and no chest pain.

options.text: Hypokalaemia
options.feedback: Hypokalaemia flattens the T wave and produces a prominent U wave — essentially the opposite appearance.

options.text: Hypothermia
options.feedback: Hypothermia produces J (Osborn) waves at the end of the QRS with a prolonged QT interval, at a normal or low temperature.

questions.explanation: Electrolyte disturbance is one of the few situations where the ECG changes management before any blood result returns.

questions.prompt: Which principle applies most directly in this educational scenario?

options.text: ECG changes of hyperkalaemia are an indication for immediate myocardial stabilisation while potassium is lowered
options.feedback: Correct. Calcium stabilises the myocardium within minutes without changing the potassium; insulin with glucose shifts potassium into cells; dialysis removes it.

options.text: Wait for the laboratory potassium before doing anything
options.feedback: With these ECG changes, treatment starts on clinical grounds. A point-of-care sample can run in parallel.

options.text: Give intravenous potassium replacement
options.feedback: That would be catastrophic — the problem is too much potassium, not too little.

options.text: A normal ECG excludes dangerous hyperkalaemia
options.feedback: It does not. Severe hyperkalaemia with a normal or near-normal ECG is well described, which is why the two are always interpreted together.

questions.explanation: Educational scenario only. Hyperkalaemia is treated according to local emergency protocols and current guidance.

explanation: Potassium sets the resting membrane potential, so a rise in extracellular potassium depolarises cardiac cells and changes the surface ECG in a recognisable sequence. Repolarisation is the first thing affected: the T wave becomes tall, narrow-based and symmetrically peaked. As the concentration rises further, sodium channels are progressively inactivated — atrial myocardium fails first, so P waves flatten and disappear, then conduction slows everywhere, prolonging the PR interval and widening the QRS diffusely rather than in a bundle branch pattern. Eventually the widened QRS merges with the T wave into a sine wave, which precedes asystole or ventricular fibrillation. Importantly, the correlation between the tracing and the serum value is poor in both directions, so a reassuring ECG never excludes dangerous hyperkalaemia.
learningObjectives: Recognise the ordered sequence of ECG changes in hyperkalaemia
Distinguish a tented hyperkalaemic T wave from a hyperacute ischaemic one by its base
Explain why the QRS widens diffusely rather than in a bundle branch pattern
State the limits of the ECG as a measure of serum potassium
clinicalContext: The ECG indicates cardiac risk; it does not measure potassium. Both the serum concentration and the tracing inform treatment, and the underlying cause must be addressed as well.

title: Flat T waves and a wave that should not be there
presentingComplaint: Five days of vomiting from gastroenteritis, now with cramps, weakness and palpitations.
history: Persistent vomiting for five days with minimal oral intake
Takes bendroflumethiazide for hypertension, which she has continued throughout
Muscle cramps and generalised weakness for two days
No chest pain; occasional skipped-beat sensations
symptoms: Constipation over the past two days
examinationFindings: Dry mucous membranes; reduced skin turgor
Regular pulse with occasional ectopic beats
Generalised muscle weakness with sluggish reflexes
Abdomen soft with sluggish bowel sounds

vitals.bedside: Dehydrated and weak. The importance of this tracing is the risk it predicts rather than the symptoms it explains.

ecg.rhythm: Regular sinus rhythm with occasional ventricular ectopic beats
ecg.pWaves: Normal, or slightly increased in amplitude
ecg.stSegment: Slight downsloping depression in the precordial leads
ecg.tWaves: Flattened, followed by a prominent U wave that can be mistaken for a T wave and makes the QT appear longer than it is
keyFindings: Flattened T waves with a prominent U wave, best seen in V2 and V3
Mild ST depression, which is non-specific in isolation
An apparently long QT interval, because the U wave is being included in the measurement
Ventricular ectopy, reflecting an unstable repolarisation substrate

interpretation: ECG changes consistent with hypokalaemia: flattened T waves with prominent U waves and mild ST depression, and ventricular ectopy. These findings indicate a risk of ventricular arrhythmia; the serum potassium and magnesium are needed to guide treatment.

auscultation.note: Normal heart sounds with occasional early beats followed by a compensatory pause — the ectopics visible on the monitor.
No murmur. The beat following a pause is louder because ventricular filling has been greater.

options.text: Sinus rhythm with ventricular ectopic beats
options.feedback: Correct — and the ectopy matters, because it is the substrate on which torsades de pointes can develop.

options.text: Atrial fibrillation
options.feedback: The rhythm is regular apart from the ectopics, and P waves are present.

options.text: Second-degree atrioventricular block
options.feedback: No P wave fails to conduct; the pauses follow ectopic beats.

options.text: Ventricular bigeminy
options.feedback: Bigeminy alternates every sinus beat with an ectopic. The ectopics here are occasional rather than alternating.

questions.explanation: Note the ectopy as part of the rhythm description — it is clinically important in a patient with abnormal repolarisation.

questions.prompt: How do you tell a U wave from a T wave?

options.text: The U wave follows the T wave, is smaller and rounder, and is best seen in V2 and V3
options.feedback: Correct. In hypokalaemia the T wave flattens as the U wave grows, so the two can appear to merge — which is exactly how the QT interval is over-measured.

options.text: The U wave precedes the QRS
options.feedback: That is the P wave. The U wave follows the T wave.

options.text: The U wave is always larger than the T wave
options.feedback: It can approach or exceed the flattened T wave in hypokalaemia, but that is a consequence rather than a defining feature.

options.text: U waves are always pathological
options.feedback: Small U waves are normal, particularly at slow heart rates and in the mid-precordial leads.

questions.explanation: Measure the QT interval to the end of the T wave, not the end of the U wave. Getting this wrong turns a normal QT into an apparently dangerous one.

questions.prompt: Why does the QT interval appear prolonged on this tracing?

options.text: The prominent U wave is being included in the measurement, and repolarisation genuinely is prolonged
options.feedback: Correct — both are true. Careful measurement to the end of the T wave is essential, and the underlying repolarisation abnormality is real.

options.text: The heart rate is too fast to measure the QT interval
options.feedback: At 82 bpm the QT interval is entirely measurable.

options.text: Bundle branch block always prolongs the QT interval
options.feedback: The QRS is narrow at 0.09 s.

options.text: It is an artefact of the filter setting
options.feedback: Filtering affects noise and baseline, not the timing of repolarisation.

questions.explanation: Prolonged repolarisation plus ventricular ectopy is the combination that precedes torsades de pointes, which is why this tracing matters.

questions.prompt: Given five days of vomiting on a thiazide diuretic, what is the most likely interpretation?

options.text: Hypokalaemia, probably with coexisting hypomagnesaemia
options.feedback: Correct. Vomiting and thiazide use together deplete both potassium and magnesium, and low magnesium makes potassium very difficult to correct.

options.text: Hyperkalaemia
options.feedback: Hyperkalaemia produces tall, tented T waves — the opposite of this appearance.

options.text: Acute myocardial infarction
options.feedback: The mild ST depression is non-specific, there is no chest pain, and flattened T waves with U waves point to an electrolyte cause.

options.text: Digoxin effect
options.feedback: Digoxin causes a scooped 'reverse tick' ST segment. She does not take digoxin — although hypokalaemia would greatly increase the risk of digoxin toxicity if she did.

questions.explanation: Always check magnesium alongside potassium. Potassium replacement frequently fails until magnesium is corrected.

questions.prompt: What is the most appropriate management principle in this educational scenario?

options.text: Replace potassium with cardiac monitoring, check and replace magnesium, and review the diuretic
options.feedback: Correct. Correct both electrolytes, monitor during replacement, and remove the ongoing cause.

options.text: Give a rapid undiluted intravenous potassium bolus
options.feedback: Rapid concentrated potassium can cause fatal arrhythmia. Replacement is given at controlled rates through an appropriate route.

options.text: Ignore the U waves as a normal finding
options.feedback: Prominent U waves with flattened T waves in this context signal a real arrhythmic risk.

options.text: Continue the thiazide unchanged
options.feedback: The thiazide is contributing to the ongoing potassium loss and should be reviewed.

questions.explanation: Educational scenario only. Electrolyte replacement follows local protocols with appropriate monitoring.

explanation: Potassium determines the rate of phase 3 repolarisation. When extracellular potassium falls, repolarisation slows and becomes non-uniform, which flattens the T wave, brings out the U wave and lengthens the vulnerable period during which an ectopic beat can trigger re-entry — the mechanism of torsades de pointes. Mild ST depression accompanies these changes but is non-specific in isolation. The practical pitfall is measurement: as the T wave flattens and the U wave grows, the two run together and the QT interval is easily over-measured. Hypokalaemia rarely occurs alone, and magnesium should always be checked, because low magnesium both promotes renal potassium loss and independently prolongs repolarisation.
learningObjectives: Recognise flattened T waves with prominent U waves as the signature of hypokalaemia
Measure the QT interval to the end of the T wave and not the U wave
Explain why abnormal repolarisation plus ectopy predicts torsades de pointes
Remember to check magnesium whenever potassium is low
clinicalContext: The ECG signals risk; it does not measure the potassium concentration. Serum potassium and magnesium, and the cause of the loss, are all required before management is complete.
